title: How Is Hungary’s New Government Doing?
gist: Four months after Péter Magyar's Tisza Party ousted Viktor Orbán's Fidesz in April 2026, the new supermajority government is rapidly dismantling Fidesz's patronage system, reforming media, resetting foreign policy toward the EU, and unlocking €16.4bn of frozen EU funds, with an improving macro picture (rate cuts, sub-2% inflation, stronger forint). Carothers judges it a hopeful redemocratization case with a collapsed opposition, but flags execution stumbles, Magyar's combative style and the risk of unmet high expectations.

insights.claim: Hungary's post-Orbán transition differs from Poland 2023, Senegal 2025 and Zambia 2021 because the ousted illiberal regime ruled unusually long (16 years) and the new Tisza government itself holds a two-thirds parliamentary supermajority and governs alone without coalition partners.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: A single-party supermajority can push reforms (EU compliance, asset recovery) far faster than coalition-bound governments, reducing Hungary-specific policy execution risk versus the Polish precedent.
insights.quote: Hungary’s redemocratization entails a distinctive combination of an enormous amount that needs to be done with an enormous amount of power to do it.
insights.locator: The New Crowd in Town

insights.claim: Prime Minister Péter Magyar is running a highly transparent, social-media-driven 'Facebook governance' style that critics deride but that keeps supporters feeling directly connected and informed.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Constant direct communication is part of how the government is sustaining popularity; watch whether it survives the slower, harder reform phase.
insights.locator: Péter Magyar was relentless and energetic

insights.claim: Hungary created a National Asset Recovery and Protection Office with broad investigative and enforcement powers to recover public assets stolen in the Fidesz years, and will join the European Public Prosecutor's Office, though actual recovery will be slow because much Fidesz corruption was legalized corruption.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
entities: National Asset Recovery and Protection Office
insights.so_what: Businesses and oligarch-linked holdings that grew under Fidesz patronage face investigation and clawback risk; expect a long legal process rather than quick recoveries.
insights.quote: a significant share of Fidesz’s corruption was cleverly designed legalized corruption
insights.locator: Taking Apart the Old System

insights.claim: By end-August 2026, sixteen Fidesz-created public interest asset management foundations had been closed and several billion euros of funds returned to the Hungarian state after their legal protections were removed.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Reclaimed assets bolster state finances and signal that entrenched Fidesz-era parallel structures (e.g. in universities, culture) are being unwound, changing counterparties for anyone dealing with them.
insights.quote: By the end of August, sixteen foundations closed and several billion euros worth of funds returned to the state.
insights.locator: A third component is getting

insights.claim: The Tisza government used constitutional changes to force out holdover officials: an amendment forcing President Tamás Sulyok's resignation, a new retirement age for Constitutional Court justices, pressure that led the prosecutor general to resign, and an eight-year cap on serving as prime minister that makes Viktor Orbán ineligible to return.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: The eight-year PM limit structurally removes Orbán-return risk, lowering tail risk of a policy reversal back to EU confrontation.
insights.locator: The second part of dismantling

insights.claim: Cutting state funding to the Fidesz-friendly media universe caused an almost immediate collapse of its propaganda echo chamber, and a June media-law amendment created an independent public media board, with a comprehensive media reform package promised later in 2026.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Fidesz-aligned media businesses dependent on state advertising lose their revenue model; Hungary's media market is being reshaped toward EU standards.
insights.locator: Media Reform

insights.claim: Government audits have publicly shown that large amounts of Hungarian cultural funding were steered to Fidesz-related people and organizations, sometimes for plainly corrupt purposes, and new people and procedures now run cultural funding.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Continuing corruption revelations keep public anger aimed at Fidesz and support the government's mandate for aggressive reform.
insights.locator: An additional area of emphasis

insights.claim: Magyar secured a political agreement with Ursula von der Leyen within weeks of taking office to release €16.4bn of frozen EU funds to Hungary (€10bn recovery funds plus €6.4bn cohesion funds); the recovery funds could be released by end-2026 if the Commission approves reforms submitted by the end-August deadline, while cohesion funds follow a separate track.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Commission approval of the recovery-fund reforms is a near-term catalyst for Hungarian sovereign spreads, the forint and domestic construction/infrastructure names.
insights.locator: Economic Reform and Restart

insights.claim: Because Hungary's budget is roughly one-sixtieth the size of the US federal budget, the €16.4bn of EU funds is equivalent in US terms to a budgetary boost of over $1 trillion.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: The scale of the inflow relative to the economy makes EU fund release a macro-significant fiscal and growth driver, not a marginal one.
insights.locator: With the Hungarian budget roughly one-sixtieth

insights.claim: Tisza's election triggered a surge in investor confidence: government borrowing rates fell within months, the National Bank cut rates three times in a row starting in June (the first cuts in over ten years), July inflation ran below 2% annualized, and the forint strengthened considerably against the dollar and euro.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Confirms the 'regime-change trade' in Hungarian assets (HUF strength, falling yields, easing cycle); watch whether disinflation holds to allow further cuts.
insights.locator: Overall, the economic situation has improved

insights.claim: Tighter spending control, lower interest rates and a stronger forint allowed the government to keep Hungary's budget deficit from exceeding 8%, after Fidesz's pre-election giveaways sent it spiraling, though the deficit remains high.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Fiscal position is still a weak point; deficit consolidation is the key risk to the bullish Hungary sovereign and currency view.
insights.locator: Thanks to tightened control of government spending

insights.claim: Hungary's manufacturing outlook has improved on business hopes for more transparent and rational business policies under the new government.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Governance-driven sentiment improvement may support FDI and industrial activity, a tailwind for manufacturers with Hungarian exposure.
insights.locator: The manufacturing outlook has also improved

insights.claim: Poor economic performance in recent years, alongside anger over corruption and decaying health, education and transport services, drove Fidesz's electoral defeat.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Incumbent illiberal governments with weak economies and visible corruption are vulnerable; a template for assessing political risk in other backsliding states.
insights.locator: Alongside public anger over corruption

themes.theme: Foreign policy pivot from Moscow to Brussels

insights.claim: The Magyar government has reset Hungarian foreign policy toward the EU, aligning Ukraine policy with the EU and in late August issuing guidelines declaring Russia's actions in Ukraine a threat to Hungary, Europe and the global order, ending Orbán's flirtations with Moscow.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Removes Hungary as a veto player blocking EU Ukraine aid and Russia sanctions, raising odds of unified EU policy on sanctions and Ukraine financing.
insights.locator: Resetting Foreign Policy

insights.claim: Some Hungary-Ukraine tension persists over the rights of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine despite the broader policy alignment.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Minority-rights friction is a residual source of Budapest-Kyiv friction that could affect Ukraine's EU accession track.
insights.locator: The main thrust of this reset

insights.claim: In June Magyar hosted the Czech Republic, Poland and Slovakia leaders to relaunch the Visegrád Group, which had gone dormant after Orbán tried to make it a platform for illiberalism.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: A revived Central European bloc could become a coordinated voice in EU budget, energy and defense debates.
insights.locator: In June, Magyar hosted the leaders

insights.claim: New foreign minister Anita Orbán (no relation to Viktor Orbán) is depoliticizing the diplomatic service, announcing the departure of dozens of ambassadors and appointing non-partisan successors.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Signals durable institutional change in Hungary's external posture rather than a rhetorical reset.
insights.locator: In addition, the new foreign minister

insights.claim: Tisza's support has risen from 53% of the April vote to over 60% in July polling, while Fidesz has fallen from 39% of the vote to around 24%.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: The government's political capital is still growing, lowering near-term political risk in Hungary.
insights.locator: After gaining 53 percent of the vote

insights.claim: Unlike Poland's defeated illiberal party, which immediately challenged the new government and made a comeback seem plausible, Fidesz is adrift: Orbán is largely absent, has named no successor, the party has no policy ideas, and senior members are leaving for business opportunities.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Low probability of an illiberal comeback reduces the risk of Hungarian policy reversals that plagued the Polish transition.
insights.quote: Fidesz no longer has any obvious levers of influence beyond its weak role in Parliament as an opposition party facing a supermajority.
insights.locator: How Fidesz Has Responded to the New Context

insights.claim: Fidesz may eventually find new political messages that regain some lost voters, but for now it presents little challenge to the government.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Opposition recovery is a longer-dated risk to monitor in polling, not a current one.
insights.locator: Thus, unlike in Poland

insights.claim: The Tisza government's speed has produced errors of judgment and execution, including a clumsy early process to select a new president and short-circuited consultation on the media law, though Magyar has shown willingness to admit mistakes and reverse botched appointments such as the justice minister.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Rushed legislation creates rule-of-law quality risks that the EU Commission could scrutinize when approving fund releases.
insights.locator: Shadows and Challenges

insights.claim: Magyar's harsh, combative style, bordering on imperiousness in Parliament and on Facebook where he has clashed with journalists, raises concern in a country emerging from years of overweening prime ministerial rule.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Personalized power is a governance risk to watch; a drift toward majoritarian overreach would undercut the investment case built on institutional normalization.
insights.quote: a harshness and combativeness that borders on imperiousness
insights.locator: In addition, while Magyar continues to impress

insights.claim: A new constitutional twelve-year limit on parliamentarians' terms, effective from the next election and without parallel in the EU, is seen by some as retribution against Fidesz rather than principled reform, and the forced ouster of the holdover president drew criticism from civic groups and international observers.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Supermajority-driven constitutional engineering could draw EU rule-of-law scrutiny even under a pro-EU government.
insights.locator: The government’s maximum force, maximum speed

insights.claim: The second phase of Hungary's transition will be defined by high public expectations and three tests: enacting comprehensive constitutional, media, education and health reforms; converting corruption revelations into successful prosecutions of former officials; and turning early economic gains into sustained improvement.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Use these three milestones (reform passage, prosecutions, growth) as the checklist for whether the Hungary turnaround trade has legs.
insights.locator: But the pressure of high expectations

insights.claim: External headwinds complicate Hungary's recovery: a regional drought hurting energy production and agriculture, Europe's stagnant economy and Russia security worries, and energy price uncertainty from continuing Middle East conflict.
insights.speaker: Thomas Carothers
insights.so_what: Hungary's macro upside is capped by energy-price and drought exposure; energy shocks remain the main exogenous risk to disinflation and the forint.
insights.locator: On top of all the internal complexities
